patient.chief_complaint: Witnessed cardiac arrest resuscitated, now unresponsive — EEG shows burst-suppression, unsure if NCSE or post-anoxic sedation
patient.history_present_illness: A 62-year-old retired firefighter was brought to the emergency department after witnessed cardiac arrest at a gym. Bystanders initiated CPR immediately. EMS arrived 7 minutes after collapse. The patient was found in ventricular fibrillation; two defibrillation shocks achieved ROSC after approximately 11 minutes of cardiac arrest. He arrived intubated with propofol 10 mcg/kg/min infusion for sedation. He is now in the ICU for targeted temperature management (TTM at 36°C). EEG was ordered by the on-call neurology resident due to concern about 'subtle limb movements' observed by nursing — periodic flexion of the left arm and subtle left facial twitching. The night team is unsure whether these movements are (A) myoclonic status epilepticus post-anoxia (malignant, poor prognosis), (B) NCSE from another cause, or (C) post-anoxic myoclonus without EEG correlate (sometimes benign, as in action myoclonus-renal failure syndrome, or sometimes malignant Lance-Adams syndrome). The patient's wife reports he had a recent syncopal episode 2 weeks ago that was worked up and 'told it was benign.' He takes metoprolol and aspirin for coronary artery disease. His cardiologist called and reports he is on amiodarone loading post-arrest. No prior epilepsy.

Prior syncopal episode 2 weeks ago — evaluated, 'benign' per wife
No prior epilepsy or neurological disease

neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 3 (E1V1M1) — intubated, sedated on propofol. No response to voice or light noxious stimuli. No spontaneous eye opening.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, sluggishly reactive to direct light. Corneal reflex present bilaterally. No doll's eye movements elicited (consistent with sedation).
neurological_exam.motor: Periodic flexion of left arm every 15-20 seconds observed by nursing. Subtle left facial twitching synchronous with arm jerks. No spontaneous purposeful limb movements. All limbs flaccid at rest between myoclonic jerks.
neurological_exam.additional: Patient intubated and on TTM at 36°C. Left arm periodic flexion at approximately 15-20 second intervals. Subtle left perioral twitching. These movements are the reason for urgent EEG consultation.

eeg.impression: This is an ABNORMAL EEG. 1. Burst-suppression pattern — generalized, with left hemisphere predominance during bursts; inter-burst intervals 4–8 seconds. 2. Left hemisphere sharp waves embedded within bursts, maximal at T3. 3. Mild EEG reactivity to external stimulation present on this recording. Electroclinical correlation: left-sided periodic limb movements time-lock to left hemisphere burst activity. Concurrent sedating medications noted (see clinical history)
eeg.limitations: Propofol infusion is noted in the clinical record; its contribution to the burst-suppression pattern cannot be excluded from EEG alone. Repeat recording after sedation adjustment may be informative.
recommended_actions: Repeat EEG after adjustment of sedating medications

output.impression: This is an ABNORMAL EEG (repeat recording). 1. Burst-suppression pattern persists — generalized, with left hemisphere predominance; inter-burst intervals now >10 seconds. 2. Left hemisphere sharp waves (T3–F3) embedded in bursts, electroclinically correlating with left-sided periodic limb movements. 3. EEG reactivity to stimulation is absent on this recording (not present on prior study). Comparison with prior study: burst-suppression pattern unchanged in morphology; inter-burst interval has lengthened and EEG reactivity is no longer elicited

output.proposed: amiodarone 150 mg IV bolus + 1 mg/min infusion (loading, current); lacosamide IV (considered AED option); levetiracetam 1500 mg IV (preferred alternative)
interactions: Amiodarone + lacosamide: MAJOR — additive sodium channel blockade causing PR prolongation, AV block, and bradycardia; amiodarone loading dose (150 mg bolus + 1 mg/min infusion) already prolongs PR to 240 ms; adding lacosamide can cause complete heart block in this compromised post-arrest heart
Amiodarone + levetiracetam: no pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic interaction; levetiracetam has no sodium/calcium channel effects — safe with amiodarone
contraindications: Lacosamide with concurrent amiodarone loading — risk of complete AV block in hemodynamically compromised post-cardiac arrest patient
warnings: Monitor ECG PR interval when combining agents with conduction effects
Agents with sodium channel blockade have additive PR prolongation risk with amiodarone
output.formulary_status: Levetiracetam IV: formulary. Lacosamide IV: formulary.
alternatives: Valproate IV as second-line if levetiracetam fails — no cardiac conduction effects; check liver function
Phenobarbital IV as third-line — no PR prolongation; respiratory depression risk

output.impression: Bilateral absent cortical N20 responses to median nerve stimulation at 56 hours post-cardiac arrest, obtained after reduction of sedating infusion. Peripheral responses (N9, N13 cervical) are present bilaterally, confirming adequate peripheral nerve conduction and technical adequacy of the study. Bilateral absence of cortical N20 responses is an established electrophysiological finding in the post-cardiac arrest setting. Clinical correlation recommended. results.title: Post-anoxic status epilepticus: treatment and prognosis
results.key_finding: In post-cardiac arrest patients, burst-suppression with electroclinical myoclonic correlates is associated with poor neurological outcomes. Antiseizure medication trials (levetiracetam, valproate) are reported in this population; evidence for neurological outcome improvement is limited. EEG reactivity and pattern evolution have been studied as prognostic markers in multimodal post-arrest assessment frameworks.

findings: Normal sinus rhythm. Normal axis and intervals. No acute ST-T changes.

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

findings: Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.
No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Post-anoxic myoclonic status epilepticus with burst-suppression EEG after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, with concurrent propofol sedation and hypothermia confounding EEG interpretation

differential.key_features: Propofol at sedating doses can produce burst-suppression; weaning trial helps distinguish
TTM at 33°C produces burst-suppression; rewarming clarifies

differential.diagnosis: Generalised periodic discharges (GPDs) on IIC, not seizures
differential.key_features: Salzburg criteria require evolution; benzodiazepine trial helps
Distinct from MSE; emerges later (days-weeks), has different prognosis
WBC 11.2 mildly elevated; no fever; sepsis less likely as primary

optimal_actions.action: Continuous video-EEG with weaning trial of propofol — distinguish drug vs ictal burst-suppression
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Burst-suppression with stimulus-evoked myoclonus; persists during propofol weaning — favors post-anoxic MSE

optimal_actions.action: Labs: CBC, CMP, glucose, Ca/Mg, AED levels, ammonia, ABG, lactate, troponin, BNP, NSE serial
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Troponin 12.8 elevated post-arrest; BNP 2840; NSE 18 elevated (HIE marker)

optimal_actions.action: Non-contrast head CT — assess for cerebral edema and exclude hemorrhage
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Diffuse sulcal effacement consistent with cerebral edema

optimal_actions.action: MRI brain after TTM rewarming — cortical and deep gray DWI patterns prognostic
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Diffuse cortical and basal ganglia DWI restriction — severe HIE pattern

optimal_actions.action: SSEP — bilateral absent N20 = poor outcome prediction
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Bilateral absent N20 specific for poor outcome (high specificity, moderate sensitivity)

optimal_actions.action: Drug-interaction check: amiodarone + AED selection + propofol
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Amiodarone QT prolongation; LEV preferred AED (avoid phenytoin); propofol weaning protocol
Rising NSE > 60 mcg/L at 48-72h predicts poor outcome

optimal_actions.action: Literature: post-anoxic MSE prognosis and treatment decisions
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MSE within 24h of arrest has very poor prognosis; aggressive treatment still indicated while multimodal data gathered

optimal_actions.action: Neurology + critical care + cardiology multidisciplinary consult

useless_tools.rationale: Amyloid PET / DaTscan have no role in HIE.
Cardiac arrest workup already includes echo; routine repeat not indicated unless specific cardiac question.

sequence_constraints.reason: ECG QTc must be reviewed before AED selection in patient on amiodarone.

critical_actions: Continuous EEG with propofol weaning trial to distinguish drug effect from ictal pattern
Load IV levetiracetam (avoid phenytoin given amiodarone + QT)
Targeted temperature management per local protocol
Multimodal neuroprognostication at 72-96h after rewarming and sedation clearance
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT make neuroprognostication decisions before 72-96h, before rewarming, or while sedation effects remain
Do NOT use phenytoin with amiodarone without continuous cardiac monitoring
Do NOT escalate to deep anesthetic infusion for GPDs alone without confirming ictal pattern
Avoid phenytoin/fosphenytoin in patient on amiodarone with HIE — additive QT prolongation and hypotension risk.
Do not make neuroprognostication decisions during ongoing sedation or hypothermia — wait until rewarming + sedation cleared (typically 72-96h).
key_reasoning_points: Burst-suppression after cardiac arrest is a multi-source signal: hypothermia, propofol, and anoxic injury all contribute — sequential weaning + rewarming clarifies
Post-anoxic MSE within 24h has very poor prognosis but treatment is still indicated while multimodal data gathered
Neuroprognostication requires multimodal data (clinical exam, EEG, NSE, SSEP, MRI) at 72-96h
Amiodarone + phenytoin is a high-risk combination — choose LEV

red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests pure drug effect, missing the underlying MSE
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Burst-suppression can be drug + hypothermia effect; persistence during weaning and presence of stimulus-evoked myoclonus argue for post-anoxic MSE

red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests prior benign event, downplaying severity
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Possible missed warning of underlying arrhythmia leading to VF arrest; relevant to cardiology workup but does not change neurological prognosis
